faq.a: A ligand is a molecule that binds specifically to a receptor protein, like a key fitting into a lock.
It's the process by which a cell converts an external signal (like ligand binding) into a functional change inside the cell.
Drugs can mimic ligands (agonists) to activate receptors or block ligands (antagonists) to prevent activation.

exam: Describe the structural components of a G-protein coupled receptor and explain its signalling pathway. — Extracellular ligand-binding domain, transmembrane helices, intracellular domain that interacts with G-protein. Activation involves GDP/GTP exchange on G-protein alpha subunit, leading to downstream effects.

A patient has uncontrolled hypertension. Discuss how membrane receptors might be involved and what drug classes could be used. — Adrenergic receptors (alpha, beta) on blood vessels and heart. Beta-blockers, alpha-blockers, calcium channel blockers target these receptors.

Explain the concept of receptor desensitization and its clinical implications. — Prolonged stimulation leads to reduced receptor responsiveness, often via phosphorylation or internalization. Important for understanding tolerance to drugs or hormones.

How can mutations in the insulin receptor gene lead to diabetes? — Mutations can cause reduced receptor number, impaired ligand binding, or defective intracellular signalling, leading to insulin resistance and hyperglycemia.
Differentiate between an agonist and an antagonist at a receptor site. — Agonist binds and activates the receptor; antagonist binds but does not activate, blocking the action of agonists.
What is the role of the transmembrane domain of a membrane receptor? — It anchors the protein within the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane, holding it in place.

In a low-resource setting, how might you infer a problem with membrane receptor signalling if specific assays are unavailable? — Look for clinical patterns suggestive of hormonal or neurotransmitter dysfunction (e.g., symptoms of thyroid disease, diabetes, or neurological disorders) and assess response to empirical treatments.

Discuss the importance of receptor polymorphisms in pharmacogenomics. — Variations in receptor genes can affect how individuals respond to medications, influencing efficacy and side effects, guiding personalized medicine.
ai.title: Membrane Receptor Proteins in Cell Signalling
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Membrane receptor proteins span cell membranes, binding extracellular signals to trigger intracellular responses. They are crucial for cell communication, mediating processes like hormone action and neurotransmission. Dysregulation is linked to many diseases.

sections.p: Membrane receptor proteins are crucial for cells to sense and respond to their environment. They act as the 'gatekeepers' for communication, allowing external signals to influence internal cellular activities without the signal molecule itself entering the cell.

b: Ligand binding causes a conformational change.
This change activates intracellular signalling pathways.
Pathways amplify the signal and lead to a cellular response.
Receptor desensitization or downregulation can occur.
sections.p: These proteins typically have three domains: an extracellular ligand-binding domain, a transmembrane domain anchoring them in the membrane, and an intracellular domain that interacts with downstream signalling molecules.

b: Drug targets: Many medications work by binding to receptors (agonists or antagonists).
Genetic disorders: Mutations can lead to non-functional or constitutively active receptors.
Infectious diseases: Some pathogens exploit or interfere with host cell receptors.
sections.p: Many diseases arise from defects in membrane receptor signalling. This includes conditions like diabetes (insulin receptor defects), hypertension (adrenergic receptor issues), and various cancers where growth factor receptors are overactive.

t.b: Identifies mutations in receptor genes, explaining inherited disorders or variations in drug response. A mutation confirms a genetic cause.
Measures receptor protein levels in tissue or blood. Low levels may indicate reduced cell responsiveness; high levels can suggest overactivity.
Quantifies receptor number and affinity for ligands. Useful in research to understand receptor density and drug binding.
